analysis.one_liner: Strips the qualified-immunity defense from civil rights lawsuits against government officials.
analysis.headline: Introduced with three Senate sponsors and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: For decades, the Supreme Court has allowed government officials, most often police, to escape paying damages in civil rights lawsuits if the right they violated was not already "clearly established" by earlier court decisions. This bill would amend the 1871 civil rights law (now 42 U.S.C. 1983) to say that good faith, a belief the conduct was lawful, or the absence of a clearly established right is never a defense. It would let people whose rights were violated by state and local officials recover money damages even when the violated right was not settled in prior case law.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are beaten, wrongfully arrested, shot, or otherwise have their constitutional rights violated by state and local government officials, and their families. Today, under the "qualified immunity" doctrine, many of those lawsuits are thrown out before any fact-finding because the specific right was not already clearly established by an earlier case. The bill also states the sense of Congress that the Supreme Court's qualified immunity doctrine misreads the 1871 statute.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new subsection to 42 U.S.C. 1983 stating that it shall not be a defense that the official acted in good faith, believed the conduct was lawful, or that the right was not clearly established at the time of the violation.
Applies to any lawsuit pending on, or filed after, the date of enactment, so people whose cases are already in court could benefit.
Declares the sense of Congress that the qualified immunity doctrine is an erroneous judicial interpretation and that Congress must restore the standard written into the 1871 statute.

analysis.who_pays: State and local government officials who violate constitutional rights could face personal liability, and the municipalities that insure and often indemnify them would bear more of the cost through settlements, verdicts, and higher liability insurance. Defendants would still be able to contest whether a violation occurred at all; the bill removes only the good-faith and clearly-established shields.

drawbacks.text: Critics argue that removing immunity entirely could expose officers and other officials to personal lawsuits for honest, good-faith mistakes made in split-second situations, potentially leading to more defensive behavior on the job.
The new defense limitations would apply retroactively to lawsuits already pending in court when the bill takes effect, changing the rules for cases that have been underway for years.
The cost of more successful civil rights suits would often fall on taxpayers through municipal indemnification and higher insurance premiums, not just on the individual officials who acted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people harmed by government misconduct, the benefit is real: today many legitimate claims die because no earlier case established the exact right in the exact way, and juries never hear the facts. The costs are also real: officials who made honest mistakes could be sued personally, and local governments and their insurers would absorb more liability. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much weight one puts on compensating victims versus protecting good-faith decision-making, and the bill takes the pro-victim side of that judgment call deliberately.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on May 22, 2025 for himself, Senator Warren, and Senator Sanders.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; the bill's action history shows no hearings, no markup, and no vote.
The bill has two cosponsors in addition to Markey, one Democrat and one independent, for three sponsors total in a 100-member Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened to the bill yet, so government officials and the municipal insurers behind them remain protected by the qualified-immunity doctrine, and people with civil rights claims still face the clearly-established barrier in court. With the bill sitting in committee with three sponsors, the practical outcome so far is that the existing legal shield stays in place.

sides.party_line_note: No one has voted on or publicly opposed the bill on the record in Congress; all three sponsors are Democrats or an independent aligned with them, and the bill has simply not moved.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and their unions
industries.note: The bill removes the qualified-immunity shield that police officers most often invoke to escape personal damages in civil rights suits. Officers who violate constitutional rights could face personal liability, which unions have consistently fought in state legislatures and Congress.

Cities and counties would face more settlements and verdicts in civil rights cases, usually paid through government funds and liability insurance. The same taxpayers who benefit from accountability bear the cost through local budgets and premiums.
More civil rights liability flowing through local governments means larger premiums and more business for the insurers that cover cities, counties, and their officials.

analysis.trajectory: This is the same three-sponsor pattern as qualified-immunity bills in earlier congresses, which never reached the floor. With only three Senate sponsors, no House companion evident in the record, and no committee action more than half a year after introduction, the realistic path is that the bill sits in the Judiciary Committee until this Congress ends unless civil rights accountability moves onto the Senate agenda in a way it has not since 2020.
